claims.assertion: There is one off-route segment on this trip: 12:46–13:07, where 9.70 km were driven where the optimal route covers 5.62 km, adding 4.08 km and reaching up to 1720 m off the optimal route (F3). Under RD-1 this segment is a route deviation and the driver's duty was, absent reasonable cause, to take the shortest and most direct route.

The whole trip ran 20.1 km against an optimal 15.5 km (+4.6 km, +30%) in 34.0 min against an estimate of 21.8 min (F1, F2), and the meter charged distance fare on 20.08 km (F6) — so the unexcused detour is what made the ride longer and dearer for the rider.

No exemption applies under RD-5: there were no in-app chat messages at all between rider and driver (F7), so there is no rider message, before the segment started at 12:46, agreeing to the route change; the driver's assertion that he simply followed his GPS (F8) is a post-trip statement, and any verbal agreement is a mere claim that does not constitute consent (G11).

No traffic exemption applies under RD-4: no traffic incidents were recorded near the route during the trip window (F12); the only band records are speed band 7 (60–69 km/h) on CTE and PIE (F9, F10) and band 4 (30–39 km/h) on Paya Lebar Road (F11), which is congestion-free on the optimal expressway route and cannot justify leaving it, and in any event band facts alone do not exempt a segment.

This being a metered RydeTAXI trip, the excess metres flow straight into the fare, and the refund is the unexcused segment's extra km at this trip's per-km rate: 4.08 km × $1.4099/km ≈ $5.75 (RD-2), consistent with the fare record's own rate of $1.4099/km derived from the distance fare of $28.31 ÷ 20.08 km (F6).

The driver's 90-day record shows 5 disputes with 3 upheld on route deviation (F15), i.e. at least one upheld route dispute within the last 90 days, so this now-repeated conduct warrants a flag_account referral alongside the refund (RD-6).

Nothing in the record raises a safety concern: the driver's statement (F8) contains no threat, harassment or dangerous-driving allegation, and weather was fair with no rain (F13), so no SAFE-1/SAFE-2 escalation is required.

weaknesses: The rider's own complaint says the driver 'never asked me', but the record contains no chat at all (F7) — the other side may argue the absence of any message means the rider simply stayed silent rather than refused, and the driver may claim an unlogged verbal agreement (F8), which we must rebut via G11 (verbal claims are not consent).

The GPS shows the deviation was up to 1720 m from the optimal route (F3) and the driver says his GPS routed him that way (F8); a judge could treat a navigation-led diversion as a lesser breach, though RD-1 sets no threshold and RD-4 is the only accepted excuse, and no incident supports it (F12).

The excess-distance refund under RD-2 is capped at the segment's extra km: the 0.52 km gap between the segment's 4.08 km extra and the trip's total +4.6 km (F1, F3) is corridor/rounding mileage that is expressly not refundable, so the driver will argue the rider's claimed 'almost 5 km back' overstates the recoverable amount.

Paya Lebar Road was recorded at speed band 4, 30–39 km/h (F11), which the driver may portray as congestion justifying the exit, even though that record concerns the road he diverted onto rather than the optimal route he left (RD-4(a)/(b)).
